title: Operating model: does everyone know who decides, who does the work and who checks it?
short: Name one accountable person for each of six core security processes and fit the whole operating model on two pages.
answer: This quarter, write down on two pages who decides, who does the work and who checks it for six core processes, from patching to exceptions, and have management approve it. Buy the work wherever that is cheaper, but keep decisions, risk acceptance and supplier oversight with your own named people.
audience: Heads of security and CISOs, IT leads who own security, and the managing directors they report to

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Give each core process one accountable name.
items.text: For patching, vulnerability management, access reviews, incident response, supplier onboarding and exceptions, name the one person who answers for the outcome and those who do the work. NIST suggests documenting who is responsible and accountable, and who is consulted and informed[^csfie].

items.title: Write down who decides what.
items.text: The BSI asks management to settle which cyber decisions need its approval[^bsicurr]. List who may accept which risk, grant which exception and isolate which system, so nobody has to ask during an incident.

items.title: Separate doing from checking.
items.text: Assurance isn't credible if the reviewer designs or operates the process, the IIA says[^iia3l]. Don't let the people who run your systems audit them or sign off their own exceptions.

items.title: Buy the work, keep the decisions.
items.text: An MSP, MDR, pentesters or a virtual CISO can do much of the work. The BSI says entities that outsource all IT remain responsible and that management stays on the hook[^bsifaq].

items.title: Fit it on two pages and get it approved.
items.text: Management approves the result and reviews roles at planned intervals and after significant incidents or changes, as Regulation 2024/2690 requires of digital providers[^ir2690]. Do it yearly and after every reorganization.

blocks.title: Write it down in two pages

items.title: Page 1, top: scope and structure.
items.text: Name the legal entities, sites and main suppliers in scope, who leads security and whether you run it central, federated or hybrid.

items.title: Page 1, middle: the RACI.
items.text: One row per core process, with exactly one A per row. If a row needs two, split the process.

items.title: Page 1, bottom: the three lines.
items.text: Who operates, who sets rules and monitors, who checks independently, and when the last independent review took place.

items.title: Page 2, top: services and decisions.
items.text: List what security offers, how to ask and how fast. Then the decision table: who accepts which risk, approves which exception and may stop which system.

items.title: Page 2, bottom: escalation and approval.
items.text: The phone chain with a deputy for each role, the next review date and management's approval. ENISA advises dating the organization chart and noting who updated it[^enisatig].

blocks.title: A RACI for six core processes
blocks.intro: A is the one person who answers for the outcome, R does the work, C is asked before and I is told after. Use your own job titles but keep one A per row.
items: **Patching.** A: head of IT. R: IT operations or the MSP. C: security, which sets the deadlines from the patching sheet, and system owners for maintenance windows. I: management, about exploited flaws past their deadline.

**Vulnerability management.** A: head of security. R: security scans, rates and tracks findings; system owners fix what patching doesn't cover. C: IT operations. I: management, monthly. Record why a finding needs no fix[^ir2690].

**Access reviews.** A: each application's business owner, who knows who needs access. R: the owner's team leads, with lists pulled by IT. C: security, for admin rights. I: internal audit. Document results and changes[^ir2690].

**Incident response.** A: head of security. R: the SOC or MDR and IT operations. C: legal, data protection and communications. I: management, the insurer and authorities as required. Business shutdowns go to the crisis team in the business continuity sheet.

**Supplier onboarding.** A: the business owner who wants the supplier. R: procurement, with a named contract manager for each contract[^iiatp]. C: security, for the tier and clauses in the third-party risk sheet. I: IT, to grant access and remove it later.

**Exceptions.** A: the risk owner, at the authority level in the risk register sheet. R: the requester, who writes the case, the compensating measure and an end date. C: security, which rates the risk. I: management, through the list of open exceptions.

blocks.title: Three lines, applied to security
items: **First line: whoever runs it.** IT operations, the MSP and application owners own the risk and operate the controls[^iia3l]. Patching and access reviews sit here.
**Second line: security.** It sets standards, monitors and challenges the first line[^iia3l]. Where security also runs the firewall or EDR, have someone else check that part.
**Third line: someone independent.** Internal audit, or an external auditor if you have none. The IIA treats 12 months between running a process and assuring it as typically sufficient[^iia3l].

**When a small company may merge lines.** The IIA ties separate lines to the risks[^iia3l], and ENISA lets IT staff take on security duties in small entities[^enisatig]. Merge the first two if you must, never the third: if size rules out an independent reviewer, 2024/2690 requires other measures to keep reviews impartial[^ir2690].

blocks.title: Central, federated or hybrid
items: **Central.** One team sets the rules and runs the security services for everyone. Choose it when one IT team runs everything.

**Federated.** Each unit has its own security officer and decides within group rules. The BSI suggests area security officers in large organizations, chosen because they know their unit's work[^std2002]. Choose it when units are separate legal entities with their own IT, since each one's management has its own BSIG duties[^bsig].
**Hybrid.** Central security owns the standards, risk register, MDR and scanning; units patch, review access and name champions. Choose it for most growing companies and for groups with plants or OT.
**Keep one register whatever you pick.** One risk register, one exception list and one incident process across units, so management sees one picture.

blocks.title: What to buy and what to keep
items: **Buy what is rare or round the clock.** The NCSC suggests outsourcing functions that are seldom used or that you lack the resources for, and notes that in-house teams know the business better[^ncscsoc]. That usually means 24/7 monitoring (see the SOC and MDR sheet), pentests and an incident response retainer.
**Put a responsibility matrix in the MSP contract.** The NCSC advises stating what the MSP does and what stays with you, including who tracks end-of-life dates[^ncscmsp].

**Know which line a provider is in.** The IIA places external providers in the line of the function that engages them[^iia3l]. A pentest ordered by IT is first-line testing, not independent assurance.

**Keep decisions, risk acceptance and supplier oversight.** Outsourcing doesn't change accountability[^iia3l]. DORA makes financial entities name a role or senior manager to monitor ICT supplier arrangements[^dora]; give every supplier an internal owner even if DORA doesn't apply.
**A virtual CISO advises, management decides.** The BSI accepts an external security officer for small companies[^std2002]; the security team sheet covers hiring one.

blocks.title: Decision rights and escalation
items: **Write a decision table.** Cover risk acceptance by size, exceptions, budget, scope, go-live against security advice and shutting down a service, each with a named decider and deputy.

**Let named delegates accept smaller risks.** 2024/2690 allows acceptance by people with the authority to manage risks, provided management gets adequate reports[^ir2690]. Set the levels in the risk register sheet.
**Pre-authorize containment.** Let the on-call engineer or MDR isolate a device or disable an account without asking first. Keep business shutdowns for the crisis team.

**Escalate on triggers.** The IIA expects a process to escalate quickly any risk that reaches an unacceptable level[^iiacyber]. Use fixed triggers: an exploited flaw past its deadline, an exception past expiry, a supplier refusing a key clause.

**Define when security must be asked.** Grundschutz++ requires involving the security officer in security-relevant projects and setting when that applies[^std3001]; the security projects sheet covers the gates.

blocks.title: Security champions in business and IT teams
items: **Start with the teams that hold the risk.** IT operations, development, finance for payment changes, HR for joiners and leavers, and plant operations for OT.
**Put their time in writing.** OWASP advises formally allocating time for champions' security work and getting management support, because formal priorities win when priorities conflict[^owaspsc].
**Give them tasks, not authority.** They triage their team's findings, review risky changes, act as first contact in an incident and pass on warnings. They don't approve exceptions or accept risk.
**Give the program an owner.** In OWASP's interviews, leading a champions program was a full-time job[^owaspsc]. In a smaller company, give it to the security lead with a fixed share of time.

blocks.title: A service catalog of what security offers
items: **List each service with how to ask and how fast.** For example: project reviews within 5 working days, supplier checks and exception decisions within 10, incident response at once.

**Cover the usual set.** Advice and project reviews, exceptions, vulnerability scanning and rating, supplier checks, incident response, awareness, and evidence for customers and auditors. FIRST groups incident-related services into event, incident and vulnerability management, situational awareness and knowledge transfer[^firstcsf].
**Name who delivers each one.** In-house, MDR, MSP or a pentest firm, so requesters know who answers.
**Say what security doesn't do.** It doesn't patch, grant access or sign supplier contracts. Name who does.

blocks.title: What the law and ISO 27001 say about roles
items: **NIS2 Article 20.** Management bodies approve the risk management measures, oversee their implementation and can be held liable; their members must follow training[^nis2].

**BSIG § 38.** Management must implement and oversee the § 30 measures and attend training regularly[^bsig]. It can't delegate that responsibility, the BSI says[^bsihand], but it can delegate the work with clear roles, reporting lines, escalation and control[^bsicurr].

**Regulation 2024/2690.** Cloud, managed service and other digital providers assign roles and report them to management, have at least one person report directly to it, segregate conflicting duties and review roles regularly. Small entities may add the duties to existing roles[^ir2690].
**DORA.** Financial entities other than microenterprises give ICT risk to an independent control function, separated from internal audit by the three lines of defense or an internal model[^dora].
**ISO/IEC 27001.** ENISA maps the roles requirement of 2024/2690 to clause 5.3 and Annex A controls 5.2 to 5.4[^enisamap], so one RACI serves both the certificate and the law.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **The IIA replaced its Three Lines Model.** The Statement of Position of 8 July 2026[^iiasop] adds guidance for organizations without separate assurance functions and says outsourcing doesn't change accountability[^iia3l]. Recheck where you've merged lines.

**Internal audit must now check cyber roles.** Since 5 February 2026, auditors giving cyber assurance must assess whether roles are established and risks escalated quickly[^iiacyber]; since 15 September 2026, also who selects, manages and monitors suppliers[^iiatp]. Expect them to ask for your RACI.

**The BSI drew the line on delegation.** Its October 2026 curriculum says the work can be delegated but not responsibility and oversight, and lists a responsibility matrix and a direct reporting line to management as evidence[^bsicurr].

**Grundschutz++ names the role conflicts.** BSI-Standard 300-1 of 20 October 2026 requires avoiding conflicts between the IT lead and the security officer, and between the data protection officer and the security officer[^std3001].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A RACI for every task.** Six core processes and a decision table settle most disputes. Add a row only when the same dispute comes back.
**An internal audit department in a small company.** Buy an independent review once a year, such as a certification audit or an auditor who neither runs nor advises on your IT.
**Reorganizing before you write it down.** Document how work is done today, then fix the two worst gaps.
**A target operating model deck.** Two pages people use beat 40 slides nobody opens.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Two accountable people for one process.** Then nobody is. Split the process or pick one.
**Security as A for everything.** If security owns patching and access reviews, IT and the business stop treating them as their job. Make the system's owner accountable.
**The admin as security officer.** The BSI warns that an active administrator in the role is likely to face conflicts of interest[^std2002].
**No deputies.** ENISA advises a deputy for each security role[^enisatig]. Name one for every A and test the phone chain twice a year.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: The managing director accepts risks and approves exceptions; the IT lead or MSP runs the controls, with first and second line merged.
Write the two pages with your MSP, including its responsibility matrix, and approve them in a management meeting.
Once a year, get a review from someone who neither runs nor advises on your IT.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Run hybrid: central rules, risk register, MDR and scanning; IT and business teams patch, review access and name champions.
Keep the security role apart from IT management, as Grundschutz++ requires[^std3001]; the security team sheet covers where it reports.
Publish the service catalog and the decision table on the intranet.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Name security officers per unit or legal entity under one group standard and one risk register.
Keep an assurance map of who checks which control, which shows gaps and duplicated checks[^iia3l].
Under DORA, document the control function's independence and the supplier oversight role[^dora].
